sum_h2: What AI radial splicing tape is
sum_p: AI radial splicing tape is a pre-cut, adhesive splice that joins two pieces of taped radial components (capacitors, inductors, LEDs and similar parts on a paper carrier) so a radial auto-insertion machine keeps feeding when one reel or ammo box runs out. Each splice is punched with holes that line up with the tape's feed holes, so the feeder's sprocket advances straight through the joint. Southern Machinery supplies it in 3-hole and 5-hole formats, in masking paper or kraft paper, with a hand splice cutter for 12.7 mm and 15.0 mm radial tape.

why_h2: A radial inserter never stops because of a hard part. It stops because a reel ran out.
why_lead: Every radial line has the same weak moment: the last component on the tape. If the next reel is joined by hand with office tape, or not joined at all, the machine waits while someone re-threads the feeder. A proper splice turns that stop into a 40-second job done while the machine keeps working.
w1d: Without a splice the operator stops the station, threads the new tape through the feeder and indexes it to the first component. Multiply that by every reel on every feeder, every shift.
w2t: Office tape does not survive the sprocket
w2d: Generic tape covers the feed holes, so the sprocket pin has nothing to drive. The joint slips, tears or jams at exactly the point where nobody is watching.
w3t: A slipped joint means a mis-pitched part
w3d: If the splice shifts the pitch by even part of a hole, the next components arrive off-centre at the cutter and insertion head. That shows up as bent leads and missing parts.
w4t: Adhesive left behind ends up in the machine
w4d: Low-grade glue oozes from the joint, picks up dust and coats guides and sprockets. Now the consumable is creating maintenance work.
w5t: Ragged cuts make every splice a guess
w5d: Cutting tape with scissors leaves the end anywhere between two holes. The splice cannot register on holes that are not there.
w6t: Consumables bought ad hoc run out at night
w6d: Splice tape is cheap, so nobody plans it. Then the night shift finds an empty box and reaches for whatever tape is in the drawer.
how_h2: Four moves at the feeder, no tools beyond the cutter
how_lead: The method below is the one printed on the source sheets for this tape. It is the same for 3-hole and 5-hole splices; the longer splice simply bridges more feed holes.
s1d: Cut both tape ends through the centre of a feed hole, square to the tape. The splice cutter does this in one press, at the right pitch.
s2d: Lift the backing paper off the splice. The die-cut liner means your fingers never touch the adhesive face.
s3d: Press the raised locating dots on the splice into the feed holes of both tape ends, so the two ends sit at the original pitch, then press down.
s4d: Fold the splice along its centre line over the other face of the tape and press. The joint is now closed on both faces and ready to feed.
how_ev: Concept illustration: tape ends joined by a 3-hole splice. Proportions are schematic, not a drawing.
how_safe: Splice at the reel or the feeder input, never inside a running machine. Follow your line's lock-out practice before reaching into any feeder path.
ill_s: Splice covers the cut and bridges the feed holes
fab_h2: What is in the splice, what it changes, and what you get
fab_lead: Six things the tape and cutter do, written the way your process engineer and your purchasing manager will each want to read them.
fab1f: High-strength, high-viscosity adhesive on a masking paper or kraft paper base.
fab1a: The joint holds against the pull of the feeder and the bend around guides, instead of creeping apart over the next metres of tape.
fab1b: Fewer jams at the splice point, so the station keeps inserting instead of waiting for an operator.
fab2f: Front and back of every splice are precision die-cut; hole size is enlarged for easy handling.
fab2a: Holes in the splice match the feed holes in the tape, so the sprocket pin drives straight through the joint and the machine can identify it.
fab2b: No mis-pitched component after a splice, which means no bent leads at the cutter and no missing parts on the board.
fab3f: Raised locating dots that seat into the feed holes of both tape ends before the splice is pressed down.
fab3a: The two ends are registered at the original pitch by the splice itself, not by the operator's eye.
fab3b: Any trained operator makes the same splice on the first try, on any shift.
fab4f: Masking paper with a no-residue, durable adhesive, or kraft paper with a coated, smooth surface.
fab4a: Masking paper releases cleanly; kraft paper's coated face slides through guides with low friction.
fab4b: You choose the backing your machine runs best on, and keep glue off guides and sprockets.
fab5f: The splice is handled by its liner, so fingers never contact the adhesive face during use.
fab5a: No skin oil or dust on the bonding surface, which is what usually weakens a hand-made joint.
fab5b: Splice strength is the same on the thousandth splice as on the first.
fab6f: Hand splice cutter for radial component tape, in versions marked for 12.7 mm and 15.0 mm tape.
fab6a: Cuts the tape end square and on the feed hole every time, which is what the splice needs to register.
fab6b: Faster splices with less training, and a joint you can trust without re-checking the pitch.

faq_h2: Questions buyers ask before the first roll
q1t: What is AI radial splicing tape used for?
q1a: It joins the end of one reel or ammo box of taped radial components to the start of the next, so a radial (vertical) auto-insertion machine or a radial tape feeder keeps feeding without being re-threaded. The splice has holes that match the tape's feed holes, so the feeder drives through the joint.
q2a: Start with 3-hole for small, light radial parts and short tape paths. Move to 5-hole for heavier parts such as larger electrolytic capacitors and inductors, or where the tape bends around several guides, because the longer splice bridges more feed holes and carries the load over more adhesive area. 6-hole is available on request.
q3t: Masking paper or kraft paper: what is the difference?
q3a: Masking paper uses a high-viscosity masking adhesive that holds well and leaves no residue. Kraft paper is also high-viscosity but has a coated, smooth surface that slides with less friction through tape guides. If you are unsure, trial both on the same feeder for a week.
q4a: Radial auto-insertion machines that run paper-carrier radial tape, including Southern Machinery's S3000 and S3010A, and radial tape feeders on SMT placement machines. Because tape suppliers differ, we confirm fit from a photo or sample of your tape before you order.
q5t: Can I use it on axial (horizontal) tape?
q5a: No. Axial tape has a different construction with no feed holes on a paper carrier. Ask us for the horizontal-insertion splice tape instead.
q6t: What does the splice cutter do, and which size do I need?
q6a: It cuts the radial tape square through the centre of a feed hole so the splice registers at the correct pitch. It comes in versions marked for 12.7 mm and 15.0 mm tape. Most radial taping uses a 12.7 mm feed-hole pitch; some larger parts are taped at 15.0 mm. Check your tape drawing, or send us a photo with a ruler and we will tell you.
q7a: Cut both tape ends through the centre of a feed hole, peel the liner, press the splice's locating dots into the feed holes of both ends, then fold the splice along its centre line over the other face and press. Do it at the reel or feeder input, never inside a running machine.
q8t: How long can I store it?
q8a: Keep rolls sealed, out of direct sun and away from heat. For Southern Machinery's SMD splice tape the published guidance is roughly six to twelve months at about 10 to 30 °C; ask us for the guidance that applies to the AI tape batch you receive.
q9t: What are the packing and lead time?
q9a: Splices come on rolls (1,000 per roll for masking paper and 500 per roll for kraft paper on our standard codes), packed by carton. Orders typically ship about 2 days after order confirmation. Tell us your monthly use and we plan the quantity with you.
q10t: How do I get a quote?
q10a: Send a close-up photo of your tape, its width and pitch, the component type, your machine or feeder model and roughly how many splices you use per month, to info@smthelp.com or WhatsApp +86 136 0256 2576. We reply with the matching codes and a written quotation.
